right: adjective
correct or true
typical: be right, the right answer/time. NOT for: direction.
You are right about the date.
That's not the right answer.
adjective
most suitable for a purpose or person
typical: the right person/tool/choice for sth. NOT for: correctness of facts.
She is the right person for this job.
Is this the right size for you?
adjective
morally acceptable or fair
typical: it is right to do sth. NOT for: practical suitability.
It isn't right to lie to your family.
Do you think it's right to report them?
adjective/adverb
on or towards the side opposite to left
typical: turn right, right hand, on the right. NOT for: correctness.
Turn right at the lights.
He writes with his right hand.
adverb
exactly, or immediately
typical: right here/now/away/in the middle. NOT for: direction.
I'll be back right now.
She was standing right in front of me.
interjection
spoken: used to get attention, agree, or begin a new topic
typical: Right, ... at the start of a sentence. NOT for: formal writing.
Right, let's get started.
Right, I'll see you tomorrow then.
noun
something you are legally or morally allowed to do or have
typical: the right to + verb, have a right to sth. NOT for: direction.
Everyone has the right to education.
You have the right to say no.
rack up: get a large number or amount of something, especially points
typical: rack sth up. NOT for: losing.
The firm racked up huge debts.
rattle off: say a list or facts quickly and easily from memory
typical: rattle sth off, rattle off statistics/names. NOT for: reading slowly.
She rattled off the names of all the players.
reach out: show people that you are interested in them and want to help or listen
typical: reach out (to sb). NOT for: ignoring.
The government failed to reach out to hard-line voters.
He reached out to his old friends.
stretch your hand or arm out to touch or take something
typical: reach out (for sth). NOT for: pulling back.
She reached out for the glass.
read up on: read a lot about something because you need to know about it
typical: read up on sth (BrE read sth up). NOT for: reading for fun.
You'll enjoy travelling more if you read up on the history.
I need to read up on the law.
rely on: trust or depend on someone to do what you expect
typical: rely on sb (to do sth/for sth). NOT for: doubting.
I knew I could rely on David.
Many people rely on the Internet for news.
depend on something to live or continue
typical: rely on sth. NOT for: being independent.
rip off: cheat someone by charging them too much (informal)
typical: rip sb off, be ripped off, a rip-off. NOT for: being fair.
I was ripped off by a taxi driver.
typical: rip sth off. NOT for: buying.
pull something off quickly and with force
typical: rip sth off. NOT for: fastening.
rope in: persuade someone to help you do something, often when they do not want to
typical: rope sb in (to do sth). NOT for: leaving alone.
I got roped in to help with the move.
round off: finish something in a suitable or satisfying way
typical: round sth off (with sth). NOT for: starting.
You can round off the evening with a visit to the club.
She rounded off the meal with cheese.
take the sharp or rough edges off something
typical: round sth off. NOT for: sharpening.
Round off the corners with sandpaper.
change a number to a simpler one
typical: round sth off (to + number). NOT for: being exact.
Round the figure off to the nearest ten.
round up: find and gather people, especially to arrest them
typical: round sb up. NOT for: releasing.
Thousands of men were rounded up and jailed.
find and gather together a group of people, animals or things
typical: round sb/sth up. NOT for: scattering.
See if you can round up a few friends to help.
His dog started to round up the sheep.
increase an exact figure to the next whole number
typical: round sth up (to + number). NOT for: rounding down.
Round it up to the nearest pound.
The total was rounded up to 100.
rub in: rub something into a surface so it goes in
typical: rub sth in. NOT for: wiping off.
keep reminding someone of something unpleasant
typical: rub it in. NOT for: forgetting.
I know I failed; don't rub it in!
rub off: remove something from a surface by rubbing, or come off a surface
typical: rub sth off (sth), rub off. NOT for: sticking.
Jack rubbed the mud off his face.
Some of the paint had begun to rub off.
start to have a feeling or habit from another person (rub off on sb)
typical: rub off on sb. NOT for: staying separate.
His good manners rubbed off on her.
I hope her confidence rubs off on me.
rule out: decide that something is not possible or suitable
typical: rule sth/sb out. NOT for: considering.
The police have ruled out suicide.
She wouldn't rule out singing again.
typical: rule sth out. NOT for: allowing.
The terrain rules out most forms of farming.
state that someone cannot take part in an event
typical: rule sb out (of sth). NOT for: including.
He has been ruled out of the match.
Injury ruled her out of the Games.
run after: typical: run after sb/sth. NOT for: running away.
He ran after her, calling her name.
The dog ran after the ball.
try to start a romantic relationship with someone (informal)
typical: run after sb. NOT for: avoiding.
He's always running after younger women.
do many things for someone as if you were their servant
typical: run after sb. NOT for: expecting help.
I can't keep running after you all.
She spends the day running after the children.
run along: used to tell a child to leave, or to say you must leave (spoken)
typical: Run along!, I'd better be running along. NOT for: staying.
Run along now! I've got work to finish.
It's late; I'd better be running along.
run away: leave a place secretly to escape from someone or something
typical: run away (from sb/sth). NOT for: returning.
Toby ran away from home at fourteen.
typical: run away (from sth). NOT for: facing.
You can't run away from your responsibilities.
He ran away from the problem.
go away secretly with someone to marry or live with them
typical: run away (with sb). NOT for: staying.
She ran away with her boyfriend.
run by: tell someone something to get their opinion
typical: run sth by/past sb. NOT for: deciding alone.
Let me run some figures by you.
I wanted to run it past you.
used to ask someone to repeat what they said (spoken)
typical: run that by me again. NOT for: understanding.
Could you run it by me once more?
run down: verb
drive into a person or animal and hit them
typical: run sb/sth down, be run down. NOT for: avoiding.
Their daughter was run down by a car.
The driver ran him down.
verb
criticize someone or something unfairly (informal)
typical: run sb/sth down. NOT for: praising.
I'm not running it down.
Don't run yourself down.
verb
lose power or energy (a battery or clock)
typical: a battery/clock runs down. NOT for: charging.
The battery ran down.
My watch has run down.
verb
gradually reduce in size or amount
typical: run sth down, run down stocks. NOT for: building up.
The company ran down its stocks.
They are running down the factory.
verb
feel tired or unwell (be run down)
typical: be/feel run down. NOT for: feeling fit.
I've been feeling run down lately.
She's run down from overwork.
verb
read or mention the items on a list quickly
typical: run down a list/the names. NOT for: ignoring it.
She ran down the list of names.
He ran down the agenda item by item.
run for: try to be elected to an official position
typical: run for president/office. NOT for: withdrawing.
run in order to reach a place or avoid danger
typical: run for the bus/cover. NOT for: walking.
run into: verb
meet someone by chance
typical: run into sb. NOT for: planning a meeting.
I ran into an old friend at the station.
He ran into her in the street.
verb
hit something or someone while moving
typical: run into a tree/a wall/another car. NOT for: avoiding.
The car ran into a tree.
He ran into a lamp post.
verb
begin to have difficulties
typical: run into trouble/problems/difficulty. NOT for: avoiding problems.
The project ran into trouble.
We ran into some problems with the budget.
verb
reach a large amount or number
typical: run into thousands/millions. NOT for: small amounts.
The cost ran into thousands of pounds.
Damage ran into millions.
run off: verb
leave a place or person in a way people disapprove of
typical: run off (with sb). NOT for: staying.
Amy's husband had run off and left her with two children.
He ran off without a word.
verb
quickly print several copies of something
typical: run sth off. NOT for: scanning.
I'll run off a few more copies.
She ran off the leaflets.
verb
force someone to leave a place
typical: run sb off sth. NOT for: welcoming.
Someone tried to run me off the road.
They ran him off the land.
verb
write a speech, poem or piece of music quickly and easily
typical: run sth off. NOT for: struggling over it.
He could run off a five-page essay in an hour.
She ran off a poem in minutes.
run off with: secretly go away with someone to live with them (disapproving)
typical: run off with sb. NOT for: staying.
Liz shocked us by running off with a married man.
He ran off with his secretary.
typical: run off with sth. NOT for: returning.
A con-man ran off with people's savings.
The thief ran off with my bag.
run out of: use all of something so that none is left
typical: run out of money/time/petrol. NOT for: getting more.
They ran out of time before the end.
no longer have enough of a quality or feeling
typical: run out of patience/energy/ideas. NOT for: having plenty.
She ran out of energy halfway through the race.
run over: verb
hit someone or something with a vehicle and drive over them
typical: run sb/sth over, be run over. NOT for: avoiding.
He was run over by a bus.
She got run over outside the school.
verb
think about something
typical: run over sth. NOT for: forgetting.
Mark's mind raced, running over the possibilities.
He ran over the events in his head.
verb
explain or practise something quickly
typical: run over sth. NOT for: skipping.
Let me run over the main points.
They ran over the plan.
verb
flow over the edge (a liquid)
typical: a bath/cup runs over. NOT for: staying inside.
The bath is running over!
The milk ran over.
verb
continue for longer than planned
typical: a meeting/talks run over. NOT for: finishing early.
The meeting ran over by twenty minutes.
The talks have run over again.
run through: verb
repeat something to practise it or check it
typical: run through sth. NOT for: skipping.
Let's run through the first scene again.
They ran through the song.
verb
read, look at or explain something quickly
typical: run through sth. NOT for: studying.
She ran through the details of the morning.
He ran through the list.
verb
be present in all of something (a quality)
typical: run through sth. NOT for: being missing.
A strong anti-war theme runs through the book.
Bad luck runs through his life.
verb
spend a lot of money quickly
typical: run through money. NOT for: saving.
He ran through his inheritance.
They ran through the cash in a year.
run up: verb
use so much of something or borrow so much that you owe a lot
typical: run up a debt/bill. NOT for: paying.
She ran up an enormous phone bill.
He ran up debts of £10,000.
verb
achieve a score or lead in a competition
typical: run up a lead/score. NOT for: losing.
He quickly ran up a big lead in the polls.
They ran up a score of 4-0.
verb
make clothes very quickly
typical: run sth up. NOT for: buying.
She can run up a dress in an evening.
He ran up a pair of curtains.
verb
raise a flag
typical: run up a flag. NOT for: lowering.
They ran up the flag.
He ran up a white flag.
rush into: do something too quickly without thinking
typical: rush into sth, rush into doing sth. NOT for: thinking first.
They rushed into buying a house.
typical: rush into a room. NOT for: leaving.
